provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: WAEC marathon: crop science
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the types of crops grown in Nigeria, explain the life cycle of a selected crop, identify common crop diseases and their symptoms, and solve problems related to crop yield calculations.
Introduction:
We have studied various crops and their characteristics in previous terms. This week we will focus on practicing past WAEC questions to strengthen our understanding of crop science.
Content:
Crop classification: We will review staple crops like maize, cassava, rice and yams as food crops, and cash crops like cocoa, rubber and cotton. For each crop, we will discuss its botany, agronomic practices and economic importance. We will also cover crop improvement through conventional breeding and biotechnology. Students will work through examples of yield calculations using farm data, such as determining the yield of maize from a plot measuring 20m by 15m with 500 plants producing two cobs each weighing 0.5kg.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to identify specimens of common Nigerian crops and match them with their botanical names and uses.
Evaluation questions:
1. List four major food crops grown in Nigeria.
2. Explain the difference between annual and perennial crops with examples.
3. A farmer harvested 200 bags of maize from a hectare of land. If each bag weighs 50kg, calculate the yield in kg/ha.
4. Describe three symptoms of maize streak disease.
Summary:
This week has reinforced our knowledge of crop science through intensive practice of WAEC past questions.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: animal science
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the classes of farm animals, explain the reproductive systems of selected livestock, identify common livestock diseases and their control measures, and differentiate between intensive and extensive systems of animal production.
Introduction:
Building on our previous knowledge of animal husbandry, this week we will focus on mastering animal science concepts through WAEC past questions.
Content:
We will review the classification of farm animals into ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats), non-ruminants (pigs, poultry), and others. For each class, we will discuss their digestive systems, nutritional requirements and management practices. Students will practice solving problems related to feed formulation, calculating feed conversion ratios, and determining livestock productivity. For example, students will calculate the feed conversion ratio for a broiler chicken that consumes 3kg of feed to gain 1.5kg in weight.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify specimens of animal feed ingredients and match them with their nutritional values.
Evaluation questions:
1. List three characteristics of ruminant animals.
2. Explain the difference between monogastric and ruminant digestive systems.
3. A farmer has 20 layers that produce 15 eggs daily. Calculate the feed conversion ratio if they consume 10kg of feed daily.
4. Describe the symptoms of Newcastle disease in poultry.
Summary:
This week has enhanced our understanding of animal science through focused practice of WAEC past questions.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: soil science
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the components of soil, explain the processes of soil formation, differentiate between various soil types in Nigeria, and solve problems related to soil fertility management.
Introduction:
We have previously studied the properties and importance of soil in agriculture. This week we will reinforce our knowledge through intensive practice of WAEC past questions on soil science.
Content:
We will review the three main components of soil: mineral matter, organic matter, and soil water. Students will practice identifying soil profiles and horizons, and understanding soil formation processes. We will discuss the major soil groups in Nigeria such as the forest soils, savannah soils, and lateritic soils, with their characteristics and agricultural suitability. Students will work through examples of calculating fertilizer application rates based on soil test results and crop requirements.
Class activity:
Students will collect soil samples from different areas around the school compound and perform simple tests to determine texture and pH.
Evaluation questions:
1. List the three main components of soil.
2. Explain how climate influences soil formation.
3. Differentiate between sandy and clayey soils in terms of their agricultural properties.
4. A soil test shows that 1 hectare of land requires 120kg of NPK fertilizer. Calculate the amount of each nutrient if the NPK ratio is 15:15:15.
Summary:
This week has strengthened our understanding of soil science through targeted practice of WAEC past questions.

topics.title: Mock examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply agricultural science concepts to solve examination questions, manage time effectively during the examination, and identify areas of weakness for further study.
Introduction:
We have been preparing for the WAEC examination through various topics and revision exercises. This week we will conduct a full mock examination to simulate the actual examination environment.
Content:
The mock examination will cover all topics in the agricultural science curriculum, including crop science, animal science, soil science, agricultural economics, and farm management. The examination will consist of theory and objective sections, structured to mirror the actual WAEC format. After the examination, we will conduct a thorough review of the questions, discussing the correct answers and common mistakes made by students.
Class activity:
Students will write the full mock examination under timed conditions, simulating the actual examination environment.
Evaluation questions:
The mock examination itself serves as the evaluation, with questions covering all aspects of the agricultural science curriculum.
Summary:
This mock examination has helped us identify our strengths and weaknesses, and provided valuable experience in managing time and answering examination questions under pressure.

topics.title: Practical marathon
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify agricultural specimens and tools, perform basic agricultural practical tasks, and record observations accurately.
Introduction:
We have learned various practical aspects of agricultural science throughout the term. This week we will focus on identifying specimens and tools to enhance our practical skills.
Content:
We will review common agricultural specimens including crops, pests, diseases, and soil samples. Students will practice identifying these specimens based on their characteristics. We will also cover agricultural tools and equipment, their functions, and proper usage. Students will work through examples of recording observations in practical notebooks, including making sketches and noting measurements. For example, students will identify specimens of common weeds in the school farm and record their characteristics.
Class activity:
Students will rotate through stations where they will identify various agricultural specimens, tools, and equipment, and record their findings.
Evaluation questions:
1. Identify three specimens of common Nigerian crops and state their botanical names.
2. Describe the function of a hand trowel in agricultural operations.
3. Differentiate between a pest and a disease in crop production.
4. List three symptoms of magnesium deficiency in plants.
Summary:
This practical marathon has enhanced our ability to identify agricultural specimens and tools, which is essential for the agricultural science practical examination.

topics.title: Weakness clinics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify their areas of weakness in agricultural science, explain concepts they previously found challenging, and solve problems related to these weak topics.
Introduction:
From our mock examinations and previous assessments, we have identified certain topics that require more attention. This week we will focus on strengthening these areas.
Content:
Based on previous assessments, we will focus on topics where students have shown consistent weaknesses. These may include areas such as agricultural economics calculations, specific plant disease identification, or livestock management practices. For each weak topic, we will provide targeted explanations, examples, and practice questions. Students will work through these topics in small groups, with the teacher providing additional support and clarification.
Class activity:
Students will form groups based on their identified weak areas and work together to solve practice questions under the guidance of the teacher.
Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the concept of opportunity cost in agricultural production.
2. Describe the life cycle of the maize weevil.
3. Calculate the break-even point for a poultry farm with fixed costs of ₦50,000 and variable costs of ₦100 per bird.
4. Differentiate between organic and inorganic fertilizers.
Summary:
This week has addressed our individual weaknesses in agricultural science, providing targeted practice and clarification on challenging topics.

topics.title: Farm project completion
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete assigned farm tasks accurately, maintain proper farm records, and analyze farm yield data.
Introduction:
We have been working on various farm projects throughout the term. This week we will focus on completing these projects and recording our observations and yields.
Content:
Students will complete all pending tasks on their assigned farm plots, including planting, weeding, fertilizer application, and pest control. We will emphasize the importance of maintaining accurate farm records, including dates of operations, inputs used, and observations made. Students will calculate yields from their plots and compare them with expected yields based on good agricultural practices. For example, students will harvest their maize plots and calculate yield in kg per hectare.
Class activity:
Students will work in their farm groups to complete all pending tasks on their plots and record their observations and yields in farm notebooks.
Evaluation questions:
1. List three factors that could affect the yield of a crop.
2. Explain the importance of maintaining farm records.
3. Calculate the yield of a maize plot measuring 10m by 10m if the total harvest is 50kg.
4. Describe three post-harvest operations for cassava.
Summary:
This week has allowed us to complete our farm projects and develop skills in maintaining farm records and analyzing yield data.

topics.title: Speed and accuracy
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer agricultural science questions quickly and accurately, manage time effectively during examinations, and improve their scores through consistent practice.
Introduction:
As we approach the final examination, it is important to develop both speed and accuracy in answering questions. This week we will focus on improving these skills.
Content:
We will conduct timed objective tests covering various topics in agricultural science. Students will practice answering questions under time pressure, with a focus on accuracy. We will discuss strategies for managing time during examinations, such as allocating specific time to each section and question type. Students will track their scores over the week to monitor improvement. For example, students will complete a 30-question objective test in 20 minutes and review their answers for accuracy.
Class activity:
Students will participate in timed objective tests, with each test becoming progressively more challenging as the week progresses.
Evaluation questions:
The timed objective tests themselves serve as the evaluation, with questions covering various aspects of agricultural science.
Summary:
This week has enhanced our ability to answer questions quickly and accurately, which is essential for success in the WAEC examination.

topics.title: Final mock
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply agricultural science concepts to solve examination questions, manage time effectively during the examination, and identify any remaining areas of weakness for final revision.
Introduction:
We have been preparing for the WAEC examination throughout the term. This week we will conduct a final mock examination to assess our readiness.
Content:
The final mock examination will cover all topics in the agricultural science curriculum, including crop science, animal science, soil science, agricultural economics, and farm management. The examination will be structured exactly like the actual WAEC examination, with the same time allocation and question types. After the examination, we will conduct a comprehensive review, discussing the correct answers and addressing any remaining areas of confusion.
Class activity:
Students will write the final mock examination under timed conditions, simulating the actual examination environment as closely as possible.
Evaluation questions:
The final mock examination itself serves as the evaluation, with questions covering all aspects of the agricultural science curriculum.
Summary:
This final mock examination has helped us assess our readiness for the WAEC examination and identify any last-minute areas for revision.

topics.title: WAEC readiness
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe effective examination strategies, prepare necessary materials for the examination, and approach the WAEC examination with confidence.
Introduction:
The WAEC examination is just days away. This week we will focus on final preparation and strategies for success.
Content:
We will review effective examination strategies, including time management, question analysis, and answer presentation. Students will prepare checklists of necessary materials for the examination, including writing materials, mathematical instruments, and identification documents. We will also discuss the importance of adequate rest and proper nutrition before the examination. Students will have the opportunity to ask any remaining questions and clarify any concepts that are still unclear.
Class activity:
Students will participate in a question-and-answer session where they can address any remaining concerns about the examination.
Evaluation questions:
1. List three strategies for managing time during the WAEC examination.
2. Describe the importance of reading instructions carefully before answering questions.
3. What materials should a student bring to the WAEC agricultural science examination?
4. Explain how adequate rest can improve examination performance.
Summary:
This week has prepared us mentally and practically for the WAEC examination, ensuring we approach it with confidence and proper preparation.
